title: Gaussian Elimination
body:
**Gaussian elimination** is the algorithm for solving a [[System of Linear Equations]]. Strip
the system down to its coefficients, use three legal moves to grind it into a triangle, then
read the answers off backwards. It is one of the few genuinely numerical algorithms the vault
has to analyse, and it is $O(n^3)$.

## The augmented matrix

Solving by hand, you keep writing the same variable names over and over. Drop them. The system

$$
\begin{align*}
2x + y - z &= 8 \\
-3x - y + 2z &= -11 \\
-2x + y + 2z &= -3
\end{align*}
$$

becomes the **augmented matrix**, coefficients on the left of the bar and the right-hand sides
on the right:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
2 & 1 & -1 & 8 \\
-3 & -1 & 2 & -11 \\
-2 & 1 & 2 & -3
\end{array}\right]
$$

Nothing was lost. The bar is bookkeeping, not notation with meaning.

## The three elementary row operations

Every one of these produces a system with the **same solution set**, which is why the procedure
is allowed to exist:

| Operation | Written | Why it is safe |
|---|---|---|
| swap two rows | $R_i \leftrightarrow R_j$ | the order you wrote the equations in never mattered |
| scale a row by $c \neq 0$ | $R_i \to cR_i$ | multiplying both sides of an equation by a non-zero constant |
| add a multiple of one row to another | $R_i \to R_i + cR_j$ | adding equal things to both sides |

The $c \neq 0$ restriction on scaling is the one people drop. Scaling by zero destroys the
equation rather than transforming it.

## Echelon and reduced echelon form

**Row echelon form** (REF):

1. any all-zero rows sit at the bottom
2. the first non-zero entry of each row (the **pivot**) is to the right of the pivot above it
3. everything below a pivot is zero

**Reduced row echelon form** (RREF) adds two more:

4. every pivot is $1$
5. everything *above* a pivot is zero too

Getting to REF is **Gaussian elimination**; carrying on to RREF is **Gauss-Jordan
elimination**. REF still needs back-substitution at the end; RREF gives you the answers with no
arithmetic left. RREF is unique for a given matrix, REF is not.

Continuing the example to REF:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
2 & 1 & -1 & 8 \\
0 & 0.5 & 0.5 & 1 \\
0 & 0 & -1 & 1
\end{array}\right]
$$

The bottom row says $-z = 1$, so $z = -1$. Substitute up: $0.5y + 0.5(-1) = 1$ gives $y = 3$,
then $2x + 3 - (-1) = 8$ gives $x = 2$. That upward walk is **back-substitution**.

## Reading the answer off

Once in echelon form, a column with a pivot is a **basic variable** and a column without one is
a **free variable**. Then:

| What the echelon form shows | Solution set |
|---|---|
| a row reading $[\,0\;0\;\cdots\;0\;\mid\;c\,]$ with $c \neq 0$ | **inconsistent**, no solutions ($0 = c$ is false) |
| a pivot in every variable column | exactly one solution |
| at least one free variable, and consistent | infinitely many, one parameter per free variable |

That maps straight onto the three cases in [[System of Linear Equations]], and it is the only
mechanical way to tell them apart for a system too big to picture.

## Elementary matrices

Each row operation is itself a matrix. Take the identity $I$, do one row operation to it, and
the result $E$ is an **elementary matrix**: left-multiplying by $E$ performs that operation.

$$
E = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\quad\text{performs}\quad R_3 \to R_3 + 3R_1
$$

Every elementary matrix is invertible, because every row operation is reversible. Two
consequences the course actually uses:

- A whole elimination is one product $E_k \cdots E_2 E_1 A$, so **row reduction is
  [[Matrix Multiplication]] in disguise**.
- If $A$ reduces to $I$, then $E_k \cdots E_1 A = I$, so that product *is* $A^{-1}$. Which is
  exactly the trick behind computing the [[Matrix Inverse]] by reducing $[\,A \mid I\,]$ to
  $[\,I \mid A^{-1}\,]$.

## Cost

Roughly $\frac{2}{3}n^3$ operations for an $n \times n$ system, so $O(n^3)$ by
[[Asymptotic Analysis]]. Worth stating plainly because the alternatives are so much worse:
[[Cramer's Rule]] by cofactor expansion is $O(n!)$, which is unusable past about $n = 10$. This
is one of the clearest cases in the degree of an algorithm choice mattering, and it belongs in
[[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]] alongside the sorting bounds.

Numerically, the pivot you divide by should be the largest available in its column (**partial
pivoting**). Dividing by a near-zero pivot amplifies rounding error, which is a floating-point
problem rather than a mathematical one, and it is why library implementations look messier than
the hand method.

## Related

- [[System of Linear Equations]] is what it solves
- [[Matrix Inverse]] and [[Determinant]] are both computed with it
- [[Basis]]: row reduction is how you extract a basis from a spanning set
